# The whole shebang

::: {.chapter-goals}
**By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:** distinguish a bioinformatics
tool from a workflow; explain the roles of Conda, containers, Nextflow,
Singularity and SLURM; and describe how they fit together without treating them
as interchangeable technologies.
:::

## Begin with the biological work

A sequencing workflow takes biological measurements stored in files and
transforms them into other files that can be checked and interpreted. Each
program normally performs one limited operation. FastQC summarizes read
quality; Trim Galore removes unwanted sequence and low-quality ends; Bowtie2
aligns reads to a reference; and SAMtools manipulates and checks alignment
files.

The programs are the analytical tools. The infrastructure around them makes
the analysis repeatable.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
    Q["Biological question"] --> I["Input files"]
    I --> T["Bioinformatics tools"]
    T --> W["Nextflow coordinates the work"]
    C["Conda or a container supplies software"] --> W
    W --> X["Local computer or SLURM executor"]
    X --> O["Checked output files"]
```

## Six technologies, six different jobs

**Conda** resolves and installs compatible software packages into an isolated
environment. It answers: *Which tool versions and libraries are available?*

**Docker/OCI** describes and builds a portable filesystem image containing the
tools and their dependencies. It answers: *What complete software environment
should travel with the workflow?*

**Singularity**—also called Apptainer in newer installations—runs container
images in an HPC-friendly way. It answers: *How can this cluster execute the
container without a Docker daemon?*

**Nextflow** models dependencies between tasks and moves files and metadata
between them. It answers: *What should run next, with which inputs, and can a
previous result be reused?*

**SLURM** is a scheduler. It assigns requested CPUs, memory and time on shared
compute nodes. It answers: *Where and when should this task execute?*

**Git** records changes to text files. GitHub stores and presents the history,
while GitHub Actions can run automated jobs after a change is pushed.

::: {.callout-warning title="A common beginner mistake"}
Conda, Docker, Nextflow and SLURM do not replace one another. A Nextflow task
may receive its software from Conda or a container, then be submitted to SLURM.
Each layer solves a different problem.
:::

## Check your understanding

For each question, name the main layer responsible:

1. A task needs SAMtools 1.19.2.
2. Five analyses are waiting for an available compute node.
3. Trimming must finish before alignment starts.
4. A collaborator must receive the same system libraries.

Answers: Conda or the container; SLURM; Nextflow; the container image.
